item.title: The Best Decks from Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok
item.description:
Disney Lorcana|competitive

The Best Decks from Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok

Wait, Detectives are good now?!

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Nov 4, 2026

|

12 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

"WHAT?! The Fates are here, and YOU DIDN'T TELL ME?!" 

Ahem, sorry. 

I think the Season of Villainy is awakening something in me. Disney Lorcana's third season of Organized Play has officially begun, overshadowing the holiday season with dastardly laughter and tinkering minions. After all, it feels so good to be bad. 

With this debut, the game has changed in more ways than one. The era of playing for those golden Mickey Mouse - Brave Little Tailor has come to an end. Instead, it's the impressive Hades - Dark Usurper who stands as the ultimate prize. As much as Mickey will always be the first, the alternative variants of Hades really do a lot for me. It's a worthy grail for aspiring players and collectors. 

There's also the introduction of Hyperia City, which has been a confusing affair to watch unfold. The cards within are clearly powerful, and ink drops redefine what's possible on each turn of the game... but there were some seriously unshakeable juggernauts at the top of the format when the set was released. Surely these cards add to those problems more than they provide a reprieve? 

Thankfully, the answer coming out of this weekend's Disney Lorcana Challenge in Bangkok was a resounding "maybe". The kingpins of the format showed up in force with a smattering of new tools, but a handful of newer archetypes also managed a breakout performance that not only puts them on the radar going forward but inspires hope that Hyperia City is far from solved. 

That's exactly the style of event I want to dig into the data for early in a season, so grab yourself a cup o' joe and settle in for a comfy selection of the best decks from Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok.

Amber Emerald Circle of Life

It seems apt to kick things off with the villain of the story, doesn't it? 

Amber Emerald was one of the known quantities heading into Bangkok, sitting comfortably as one of the top decks in the format. Despite that, two copies of the deck would meet in the finals to play for all the marbles. 

Fellow content creator Avery from Quest For Two would manage to conquer the event with their traditional spin on the deck, so let us take a closer look at the tools that got it done. 

BloodthirstyAvery's Amber Emerald Circle of Life - 1st Place at Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok

Avery's deck was lovingly named "Doing His Part" — in reference to the snazzy piece of tech for the weekend, Aladdin - Doing His Part. None of the other Circle of Life decks in the top sixteen featured any copies of Aladdin, with many further down featuring one or less. The three copies presented here provided a strong hedge against the various Retro Evolution Device decks and happened to come up big against the breakout Ruby Emerald decks built around Rivera Family Photo and The Torn Corner.

This is very much a case of "If it ain't broke, don't fix it" as far as I'm concerned. Avery's list featured exactly two cards from Hyperia City: Don Karnage - Debonair Pirate and Above the Crowd. The former is an exceptionally well-stated threat that both eliminates opposing characters and prevents the opponent from racing, while the latter is just a clean spot removal effect for any problematic glimmer that needs to be shut down on your way to Prince Phillip - Vanquisher of Foes.

Otherwise, the deck hasn't changed much from other recent iterations. Your primary goal is to set up a board of efficient singers that are difficult for the opponent to remove, then leverage them to enable one-sided board wipes that take over a game. At that point, it's fairly trivial to quest out to get over the line. 

The most infamous of these is the pairing of Malicious - Mean and Scary and Circle of Life. If you manage to ditch a Prince Phillip - Vanquisher of Foes with either Tod - Clever Fox or Strike a Good Match, you can sing both songs in the same turn to pile damage into the opposing board and sweep it all away. This isn't too dissimilar to how Under the Sea used to operate in Amber Emerald Dogs — it just takes the game away. 

If you need something a little faster, you can rely on the package of Malicious, Mean and Scary, To Wither a Flower and Max Goof - Rebellious Teen instead. If you can establish a character with Singer 4, you can hardcast Malicious, Mean and Scary before singing To Wither a Flower to deal three damage to every opposing character. You can achieve this as early as turn three, or weave either version of Max Goof into the sequence somewhere to up the total board wide damage. 

The final nail in the coffin is Milo Thatch - Getting His Hands Dirty, who serves as another potent target for Circle of Life. If you use "Scholar's Gambit" on the turn Milo is reanimated, you guarantee yourself a drawn card from "Practical Knowledge" at the end of the turn. Ward + Bounce is a terrifying combination to handle, especially if you've just had your board annihilated, and it isn't uncommon for Milo to be kept safe by Ward long enough to ferry in a chunk of card advantage. 

The majority of differences between lists at this stage come down to tech choices, but it is worth noting that finalist Nobita was rocking a full four copies of the new Max Goof - Karaoke Star. A shift target that filters away dead songs and quests out incredibly fast? I do wonder if it's good enough to make the cut in future. 

Amber Sapphire Detectives

Amber Sapphire Detectives was beginning to feel like the worst kept secret in Disney Lorcana as DLC Bangkok got closer. There were plenty of doubters that didn't think the deck had what it takes, but if you were in the playtesting trenches you knew ball. 

This archetype has been cooking in the background and has finally reached critical mass with Hyperia City. Somehow, this character-focused aggressive deck is packed with interaction. It can even leverage ink drops to reach all the way to Raging Storm! 

FL-rui's Amber Sapphire Detectives - Top 4 at Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok

Yup, that's six different versions of Judy Hopps. What can I say? They breed like rabbits. 

The name of the game here is synergy. In a vacuum, your cards are weaker than your opponents, but as they begin to snowball, they become more than the sum of their parts. This trend started back in Whispers in the Well with Detective-focused payoffs like Judy Hopps - Uncovering Clues and Fangmeyer - Icy Officer, but it's been dialled to eleven with the support in Hyperia City. 

Elisa Maza - Hardworking Detective is disgusting. Sure, the stats are slightly below rate, but this style of targeted discard is the best way to proactively eliminate your opponent's best answers to your slowly snowballing board, all while providing you with perfect information about your opponent's plays. You needed to know if the Prince Phillip combo was in hand? Elisa has you covered. 

It's a similar story for Nick Wilde - Toy Drive Officer, who just does everything that this deck wants to do. Amber Sapphire is uniquely stuffed with big butts to get the best out of Support, while Nick himself rewards you for the selection of cheap characters you already wanted to play with a smooth flow of card draw. Judy Hopps - Day Camp Instructor and Judy Hopps - Always Vigilant are similarly picky about playing a character in the same turn, so your deck is built to make sure it isn't difficult to keep Nick enabled. 

Speaking of, Judy Hopps - Always Vigilant is nasty enough in its own right. Gaston - Superior Archer was already a format-defining piece of interaction, yet Detectives get eight copies of the effect — one of which is cheaper AND searchable! — to lean on. Shift 2 is often backbreaking in making sure that another character has been played, and it isn't uncommon to slam Gaston and Judy in the same turn to completely swing a board that Prince Phillip thought was locked up. 

Detectives wasn't the only way to play Amber Sapphire this weekend either, with the Princess Ramp variant also finding a top eight finish in the hands of an Illumineer named Glenn. As somebody who was already watching the evolution of this deck like a hawk, I'm ecstatic. It's a darn good time to be a fan of yellow and blue, and I cannot recommend that you try out both deck lists any more than I would right now. 

Emerald Steel Midrange

While Jake Quinsee and Joseph Quigley both managed a top eight finish on Emerald Amethyst Retro Evolution Device, it somehow wasn't even the second most-popular recurring villain in the top cut. 

You didn't think Emerald Steel was going to disappear overnight, did you? 

Thiago Santana's Emerald Steel - Top 4 at Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok

I said the same thing about Amber Emerald: If it ain't broke...

Thiago Santana's top four list perfectly encapsulates what we've grown to know and love about Emerald Steel: a wall of cheap threats, a dash of resist, and the backbreaking power of Elinor - Renowned Diplomat. If you were unclear about how important Strength of a Raging Fire is to the "curve-out-and-go" Steel deck, we've even got three copies of Max Goof - Rebellious Teen in the deck despite only having one target. 

The biggest innovation here is the movement away from the Darkwing Duck package to facilitate the shiny new pair of two-cost Steel characters from Hyperia City. Flash - Efficient Clerk has a premium stat line with a situational powerful effect that shuts down upcoming players like Mulan - Martial Arts Master.

Toulouse is the real gold standard upgrade though. 'Pete - Games Referee but smaller' is still a format-defining card, and these aggressively slanted decks are the best place for it. Not only is the body worth more, but most opponents are relying on cheap actions to slow you down and allow their card quality to outclass yours. Toulouse shuts those out with ease and can be timed to perfection with the help of Ursula - Deceiver. 

The more that Circle of Life and Mean, Malicious and Scary cement themselves as the benchmarks of the format, the more I find myself wanting to play a Steel deck with Toulouse. If I had a big tournament tomorrow? I think this deck is where I'd be. 

Emerald Ruby Family Photo

Finally, I wanted to chat about the coolest deck that managed to make the Top 16 in Bangkok. There were endless whispers about the potential of Rivera Family Photo and The Torn Corner after they were revealed in Hyperia City, I just hadn't seen the shell come together for them yet. 

I thought it would be another Amber Circle of Life shell, but it seems that Emerald gets the nod because of those infamous Prince Phillip - Vanquisher of Foes combos. 

BTD_Arnold_ pe's Ruby Emerald Family Photo - Top 16 at Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok

It might feel more apt to refer to this as Emerald Ruby Actions, given those are the most prominent part of the deck. Emerald Ruby is looking to get a critical mass of cards into the discard to enable gigantic payoffs like Olaf - Snowman of Action and Rivera Family Photo, both of which offer their own engines that make them flourish.

Rivera Family Photo continuously moves two cards from your deck into the discard, which simultaneously fills the discard for Olaf, activates Lyle Tiberius Rourke - Adventurer for Hire and The Leviathan - Guardian of Atlantis on demand, and provides you with a way to cheat The Torn Corner into play. 

Even better, it offers you inevitability. Once you've swept away your opponent's threats, it will slowly and methodically gain you all the lore you need. Between all the board wipes and incidental draw from The Torn Corner, you have a shocking amount of staying power. 

This is also the perfect home for Max Goof - Karaoke Star. You have an excess of songs to discard, it helps activate your discard-focused cards, and it'll regularly quest for four as your discard fills up. It's just a custom card for this archetype and you're never unhappy to see it. 

Another Tale to Spin is a meaningful consistency piece in that regard too, offering you another cheap song that accelerates towards your big The Leviathan - Guardian of Atlantis turn, but can be happily discarded to Max Goof, Tod - Clever Fox or Strike a Good Match once the work is done. 

I also wanted to highlight the really cool synergy between Olaf - Snowman of Action and Retro Evolution Device. Olaf usually costs a minimal number of resources by the time it hits the table, and "Chaotic Collision" should stabilize you as it does. Once you do so, you can cash Olaf out to the Retro Evolution Device to immediately cheat out a Prince Phillip - Vanquisher of Foes or The Leviathan - Guardian of Atlantis. 

This often leads to spots where the opponent thinks they're safe from the whammy when they're absolutely not. It's very sweet and I highly recommend giving it a shake. 

Closing Thoughts

I'm overjoyed to see the Core Constructed format evolving into a mixture of old stalwarts and new blood. That's everything I want from the early events following a set release. Hyperia City has got things looking really sweet and I have no doubt that Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok is just the beginning. 

Have further questions? Let me know over at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky! Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game.

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing!

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!

item.title: The Best Rogue Advanced Decks in Yu-Gi-Oh Right Now
item.description:
Yu-Gi-Oh!|Advanced|competitive

The Best Rogue Advanced Decks in Yu-Gi-Oh Right Now

Yu-Gi-Oh's biggest banlist ever and another game-changing set mean there's plenty of room for rogue decks to win.

By Hanko Chow

|

Published Nov 11, 2026

|

9 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: YuGiOh Metagame Recap

After the latest Advanced banlist update, the metagame is finally diverse again. There are inevitably going to be some strategies that are broken when uninterrupted, but also capable of making strong half-boards against hand traps, while also having enough power in their cards to play against an established field.

The decks that feature Medius the Pure and the newest Power Patron faction - the Ars Magnas - are the decks to beat. That is, until Magnificent Maestros releases this week. Angelechy's newest support from Beyond the Brave has also helped establish it as a top-tier strategy with its stun like playstyle and huge damage potential. Even with these strategies running rampant, you can't count out other decks like Invoked, Fairy Tail or Radiant Typhoon, and of course Light and Darkness Ritual is still busted since their boss monsters are nearly invincible.

The Best Rogue Advanced Decks Right Now

Now that YCS Orlando has concluded, let's talk about some of the best Rogue strategies to keep an eye out for before the release of Magnificent Maestros.

Blitzclique is Good For Advanced Too!

Jumping back into the Advanced format after testing a lot of Genesys hasn't been that easy, but luckily I still have my Blitzclique cards and they're honestly not that bad in Advanced either. While Blitzclique may not be a one-card combo deck, they can snowball into an insane amount of advantage very quickly when you can trigger all the searching and recursion with the Spells. It just goes to show how broken Whisker Blitzclique is, even at the Advanced format power level.

This list is pretty cookie cutter compared to the ones topping Regional level events, many of which are playing either Dominus Purge or Nibiru, the Primal Being over Fydraulis Harmonia. It's an understandable choice, but I wanted to increase the odds of opening up the devastating Crackle Blitzclique and Whisker Blitzclique combo, which can also be created by using Crackle Blitzclique to summon Surge Blitzclique and then having Surge witness a card being destroyed either by your very own Ghost Ogre & Snow Rabbit or Fydraulis Harmonia. This may seem a bit of a stretch since it's a three-card combo, but you would be surprised at how frequently it shows up!

Blitzclique Overvolt is actually rather underrated. At first, the card seems lackluster and unnecessary, but after practicing a combo that starts with Blitzclique - Breakaway and any Blitzclique card or Blitzclique - Breakaway and Grain Blitzclique, I realized how often you need Grain to search for a card that can destroy to trigger Surge for another search. It's an impeccable board-breaking tool since you don't mind it getting negated and can easily add it back to your hand to play it again!

Time will tell if Blitzclique still has what it takes to stay in the metagame as we head into Magnificent Maestros. I think as long as you have enough cards like Trap Eater to respect Mind Scan, then I think it has a chance.

Time to Face Your Destiny

The next most underrated support cards from Beyond the Brave would have to be the Destiny HERO cards since they actually can be played as a mono-attribute strategy compared to the classic "Omni HERO" deck we've seen in the past years. Destiny HEROs featuring a small Masked HERO package has been seeing a ton of play at local and Regional levels and I think it has a lot going for it, even in such a compact deck.

This version of HEROs is built very differently compared to the "Omni HERO" deck you've seen before. It's built on the classic philosophy of multiple one-card combo starters and a ton of hand traps to have better odds against opponents. Since the deck is limiting itself mostly to Dark monsters, it can take advantage of powerful hand traps like Dominus Impulse and even Dominus Spark. Just be wary that Winged Kuriboh Sabatiel LV10 is a Light monster so it might conflict with Dominus Impulse.

There's a ton of searching going on in this deck, with so many cards being able to bridge to one another. I really like how they even brought back Destiny HERO - Dreadmaster and Clock Tower Prison retrained with the new Dark City at Midnight. Fun fact, Destiny HERO - Dreadmaster has a secret broken summoning lingering or "unclassified" effect. After you Special Summon Dreadmaster, all your Destiny HERO monsters can't be destroyed and you don't take any Battle Damage. It doesn't protect Xtra HERO Cross Crusader, but making Destiny HERO - Destroyer Phoenix Enforcer and Destiny HERO - Plasma indestructible can be game winning on it's own.

If you have room in your Extra Deck for Linkuriboh or Relinquished Anima, I'd suggest squeezing them in for the Destiny HEROs matchup. Destiny HERO - Dark Angel is an incredibly annoying Spell lock that they can set up and summon to your field. But it's extremely easy to out if you just carry those Link 1s in your Extra Deck. Otherwise, they'll make sure the Dark Angel stays on your field and all your Spells will be useless against them.

Atlantis Strikes Back

Another Beyond the Brave strategy that's starting to make waves (pun intended) is the new Atlantis strategy. It's another deck that can play with the Ash Blossom & Joyous Spring and Dominus Impulse hand trap line up which has been a powerful combination over the years. Players are still trying to solve the Water strategy since there are just so many ways to build and play with it, but Chris Foose managed to finish in the Top 8 at the South Park regionals with his take on the new Atlantis deck by focusing only on the new Atlantis cards with a small Atlantean package.

This deck aims to play with 15 starter cards for its engine while packing 16 of the best hand traps in the game. These kinds of ratios are a classic take on modern deck building and really showcases the best part of these new Atlantis cards.

You won't see this version of the deck in Genesys format since it's actually a Link climbing strategy. If you don't have access to Atlantis, City of the Sea Dragon, then you'll need to make Marincess Coral Anemone to help Link climb into the Link 3 Levia-Dragoon - Daedalus. This Link 3 summons another from the deck which helps you climb into the Link 4 Azure Ocean Dragon Lord - Neo-Daedalus Rage which is basically Soul Charge on summon but you can't summon any more afterwards.

The theme of this deck is that all the new Atlantis monsters are treated as the classic "Umi" which helps facilitate their card effects since they usually require an Umi on the field to activate. Over the years, Levia-Dragon - Daedalus has been wreaking havoc by sacrificing Umi for its board wiping effects, and these retrained versions of it are similar with the Link-4 having a board wipe effect that doesn't affect cards that are treated as Umi. The one-sided Card Destruction effect from Levia-Dragoon - Daedalus is interesting since it cannot be chained to with its condition, making it so you can't take advantage of it with Droll & Lock Bird.

Of course, you can't forget about Monster Arms of Atlantis, which is basically a monster effect negation while it's in your field or graveyard, making it very difficult to interact with since it can hide in the graveyard while defending your Link climbing strategy from the likes of Nibiru. Daedalus Maelstrom is also very powerful going first or second since it's a Counter Trap you can set up going first, but also a removal effect in the graveyard you can send going second with Siren Vortex of Atlantis, guaranteeing you some value in both scenarios.

I was hoping this deck could play with some of the older Umi support cards like Ocean Dragon Lord - Kairyu-Shin and Kairyu-Shin's Dark Reef since these cards are pretty powerful, but Chris built a smooth list that keeps it short and simple without overcomplicating the deck, from Link Climbing options to Synchro options with First Penguin and even Rank 3 and Rank 7 options depending on the situation. Keep in mind that Atlantis, City of the Sea Dragon does reduce all the Levels of monsters in the hand and field by one!

Phantom Knights Are Just Getting Started

Another deck that can play with the Ash Blossom and Dominus Impulse pair which may see more play after Magnificent Maestros is Phantom Knights. This Dark Warrior deck received more support from Chaos Origins but was left lacking due to the power level of the other top tiers at the time. Now, in this new post-ban era of Yu-Gi-Oh, it looks like it has a chance since Alexander Martin managed to win the Dutch Open with it last week!

This deck revolves around using Phantom Knight monsters to search each other, filling the graveyard with monsters which have effects you can use or the Traps that reborn the Phantom Knight monsters which you can recycle with Shamanite Shamanknight and The Phantom Knights of Malevolent Scythe. Currently, its win conditions are revolving around using the Rank-Up-Magics to summon out the monster-negating Dark Requiem Xyz Dragon or winning games with the massive amount of ATK power from Arc Rebellion Xyz Dragon. Otherwise, it can surely win off of just card advantage since it can accumulate a bunch from all the searching effects with The Phantom Knights of Malevolent Scythe and The Phantom Knights of Rusty Bardiche.

Exosister Karmael may seem strange in Phantom Knights but it's actually something you can summon via The Phantom Knights' Rank-Up-Magic Launch since it can summon any Dark Xyz on top of another Dark Xyz with no Xyz Materials and a rank lower. Karmael isn't necessarily an omni-negate, but changing the effect of your opponent's Monster or Normal Spell/Trap effect is basically like an advantageous negate.

You might see Phantom Knights more often with the release of Magnificient Maestros since we're finally getting the new Dark Rebellion Xyz Dragon, Four Heavenly Dragons imported to the TCG, allowing the deck to summon Exosister Karmael more often as well as other Rank 4 Dark options like Evilswarm Ophion to prevent decks that need to Special Summon Level 5 or higher monsters. You also can't forget that Dark Rebellion Xyz Dragon, Four Heavenly Dragons is also another board-breaking effect on summon, allowing Phantom Knights more removal effects after using The Phantom Knights of Break Sword.

Magnificent Maestros Waiting Room

We're just days away from another game-changing set. I wonder if Toons are really as strong as what players are saying, but I think if you're prepared for Toons and stop Perfect Toon World with cards like Veidos the Eruption Dragon of Extinction, PSY-Framegear Delta or even Ghost Ogre & Snow Rabbit, then maybe you'll have a chance. Just watch out for Funny Dark Rabbit.

The other new cards are also just as exciting from Blue-Eyes support to Unchained and the long awaited Witchcrafter support! I just hope that they also announce a new Genesys points update before this upcoming weekend as I'll be at the Toronto Regionals. Not sure what my plan is yet since this new set is sure to impact both the Advanced and Genesys format, but I'm sure I'll figure it out by then!

item.title: Manipulate the Battlefield With Reality Fracture's Denzilore Fatehold in Commander
item.description:
Magic: The Gathering|Commander|casual

Manipulate the Battlefield With Reality Fracture's Denzilore Fatehold in Commander

Scry me a river.

By Tyler Berger

|

Published Nov 11, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Commander Bestiary

The Commander Bestiary returns with another deck guide from Reality Fracture! You'd already know that if you were today's commander: Denzilore Fatehold, the prophesying sphinx! We'll be using our knowledge of the future to shape our gameplan, picking the best cards for any situation.

The Dean of Fatehold

Denzilore Fatehold is one of the five elder sphinxes that founded Hexhaven, the alternate reality version of Strixhaven in Jace's Echoverse. The Fatehold school is an alternate to Lorehold – where Lorehold looks to the past, Fatehold studies and attempts to manipulate the future. 

To look to the future in Magic terms, you'll use effects that scry and surveil. Whenever you do, Denzilore will put a +1/+1 counter on each creature you control! There are tons of effects to scry and surveil, often repeatedly, and Denzilore will put those to work by quickly reducing your opponents' life totals. Since Denzilore has flash, you can even use him as a combat trick in a pinch. 
While putting counters on your whole board is powerful, a few counters isn't going to end a game. To maintain pressure, we'll be going all in on the scry and surveil plan. It's surprisingly easy to find cards that incidentally scry or surveil as a little bonus, like Gods Willing, and about a third of our deck today does one or the other – even some of our lands! Many of these are repeatable effects to make sure our creatures keep scaling. 

The blue and white color pair isn't typically known for being an aggressive one, and your supporting cards might show that. There's many cards like the aforementioned Gods Willing, and plenty of cantrips like Consider, but those aren't really advancing your game themselves – they only become aggressive cards with Denzilore in play. You'll want to use Gods Willing and the like to keep your commander safe and keep the damage coming.

Since Denzilore puts a counter on each of your creatures, you're best playing him in a go-wide creature strategy. Lots of creatures means lots of +1/+1 counters, so every scry and surveil gets better with additional bodies on the field. Blue and white are great at playing a bunch of little flying creatures, many of which scry and surveil on their own. 

You could also play Denzilore as more of a Voltron strategy. While starting as a 3/4 flying isn't incredible, your commander's stats will quickly increase. Suit him up with cards like Sword of Once and Future and Aqueous Form and you'll be dealing lethal commander damage in no time.

Drawing Cards and Becoming the Problem (As Garfield Intended)

Denzilore doesn't lend himself to many combos by himself – he's more about using the future to punch his enemies. That said, he's got one that's uniquely "Fatehold". You'll need Sigiled Starfish, a creature that can tap to scry. Pair that with Matoya, Archon Elder, which gives you a draw every time you scry or surveil. The final piece is Mind Over Matter, which lets you discard a card to untap a creature (among other things).

So, you'll tap your Sigiled Starfish to scry. Matoya will draw you a card. You'll use Mind Over Matter to discard a card to untap the Starfish. Repeat as much as you like to draw any number of cards, discarding one each time. If your commander is on the field when you do this, you'll add a +1/+1 counter to all your creatures every time you repeat the loop!

How to Play Denzilore Fatehold in Commander

What's the best thing about building around the scry and surveil mechanics? Those cards are perfectly useful even without your commander in play, because they're still manipulating your next draw toward what you need. If you run out a turn two Nightveil Sprite and start poking for one damage, you're also making sure you hit your land drops and pick up useful cards while you're getting set up. 

You'll want to get these kinds of creatures in play before you cast Denzilore, so you can immediately get some +1/+1 counters once he hits the board. A creature like H.E.R.B.I.E., Lovable Robot will provide utility before and after Denzilore hits the field, and becomes a beefy flying attacker after your commander gets to work. 

You've got a few engines to repeatedly scry/surveil, and you'll probably want those online before you cast your commander. Proctor of Potential surveils every time a creature enters, so you can even get an immediate trigger from Denzilore himself. Thassa, God of the Sea is a simple way to scry every turn and make a creature unblockable, and Retreat to Coralhelm gives a scry with every land. 

On top of your repeatable engines, a huge portion of your cards have little scry and surveil bonuses attached. You've got all the various Consider, Opt, and Serum Visions style cards to filter through your deck. Your interaction cards like Sheltering Light and Dissolve give a scry. Several of your lands, including the upcoming Star Trek lands Federation Outpost and Ni'Var Science Academy, have free surveils attached.

The next batch of cards take advantage of all the +1/+1 counters you're distributing with Denzilore. You've got one-sided board wipes with Damning Verdict and Wave Goodbye, and an incredible protective card with Ripples of Potential. Your +1/+1 counters fuel your card draw with Danny Pink and Biorganic Carapace.  

 

At your top end, you've got some big scry/surveil payoffs. Saheeli, Consul of Oversight crafts a Thopter token once each turn when you scry or surveil. You can save instant speed effects like Consider and Sigiled Starfish to trigger this ability on opposing turns, and you can stack the trigger so Denzilore will add +1/+1 counters after each new Thopter hits the field. Triumph of Saint Katherine is awesome here, with so many ways to know ahead of time when you're going to have a miracle. The lifelink is great with Denzilore strengthening it, and if Triumph dies and shuffles into your top seven cards, all the scry and surveil cards will help drag it to the top again. 

Planetarium of Wan Shi Tong is your most expensive card at six mana, but the reward is enormous. Not only does the Planetarium let you scry 2 every turn, but you also get to play a free card each turn when you scry or surveil! 

To close out the game, you've got a few ways to make that final push. Yoshimaru, Beloved Companion and Lae'zel, Vlaakith's Champion both effectively double Denzilore's counters. Herald of Secret Streams and Abzan Falconer give your squad evasion to declare an alpha strike. The funniest, and yet surprisingly powerful, is Cryptic Annelid. This weird little uncommon has you scry, then scry, and then scry again! That's three separate instances for Denzilore and your other effects, leading to some crazy triggers from just casting this strange little worm guy. Playing Denzilore in Commander does feel like you're playing Limited a bit, since so many of the cards don't seem individually strong yet complement Denzilore so well. 

You can always soup this deck up even further, if you've got the budget. Esper Sentinel is good on its own, and nobody will pay the tax once you've put a few +1/+1 counters on it. Elspeth, Storm Slayer can either generate two bodies every turn for Denzilore to put +1/+1 counters on, or she can add more +1/+1 counters of her own while granting flying. Finally, no +1/+1 counter deck is complete without The Ozolith! That gives you insurance against any removal, and threatens lethal commander damage if you pile a bunch of counters on it.

Thanks for joining us for this edition of the Commander Bestiary! We have even more from Reality Fracture to enjoy, including the other Elder Sphinx legends, and plenty of Star Trek legends are on the horizon! item.title: Dragapult ex/Crushing Hammer Deck Guide (Pokémon TCG)
item.description:
Pokémon|competitive

Dragapult ex/Crushing Hammer Deck Guide (Pokémon TCG)

Crush your opponent's dreams with a coin flip.

By Natalie Millar

|@nataliem9999
|

Published Nov 11, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Pokémon Deck Guides

Hello everyone! Dragapult ex with Crushing Hammer is currently the undisputed best deck in the format, and that's looking to remain true in the Delta Reign format. The 60 cards below have already won two Regional Championships and I wouldn't be surprised if it won another major tournament prior to rotation!

Dragapult ex/Crushing Hammer Deck List

This deck looks very simple but it has a wide variety of game plans. The core of the deck is the Dragapult line; Drakloak's Recon Directive ability filters through your deck and Dragapult's Phantom Dive is one of the most powerful attacks in the format, setting up spread damage and multiple knockouts. The cards in the Dragapult deck are so efficient that you have a ton of deck space to play many luxury cards, which has resulted in the default version of Dragapult ex playing four copies of Crushing Hammer. Crushing Hammer looks a little strange when it's a flip card, but many decks in the current format rely heavily on their attachments for turn and hitting an early Crushing Hammer heads will reliably buy you a whole turn against the aggressive decks. Crushing Hammer also allows you to have an alternate win condition of resource denial and to sometimes act as a control deck. This deck is one of the best users of Budew's Itchy Pollen, which prevents Items and slows down the opponent in the early game.

Because of the Fire and Psychic cost of Phantom Dive, you're incentivized to play Energy acceleration Supporter cards like Crispin and Rosa's Encouragement in this deck. This gives you the extra attachments to take advantage of Munkidori's Adrena-Brain, which is arguably the strongest card in the format. There are several scary Stadium cards in the format like Battle Cage, Legendary Pyroduct and Nighttime Mine, but your counter Stadium Risky Ruins also doubles as your win condition since it damages your Pokémon when they come into play, enabling you to move the damage over with Munkidori. This deck also has the room for a 1/1 line of Dudunsparce with Run Away Draw, which both is extra draw power and is a way to win in stalled game states since you can continuously loop a Pokémon coming into play to add an extra 20 damage to your opponents board.

The rest of the cards in this deck all have the goal of enabling your game plan. Three Night Stretchers recover Pokémon and Energy to rebuild your setup against early knockouts, Meowth ex and Fezandipiti ex get you out of mediocre hands, and you have the 11 Pokémon Search Items to set up your board.

One of the most underrated aspects of this deck is the flexibility of attackers. There are many scenarios across different matchups where you can attack with Munkidori's Mind Bend or Fezandipiti's Cruel Arrow, and some matchups where Cruel Arrow is your primary game plan to avoid losing to Lillie's Clefairy ex's Fairy Zone ability. Boss's Orders is both used as aggression but also as an Energy denial card, as you can sometimes Boss up an opposing Meowth ex to deny your opponents next attachment, acting as an additional Crushing Hammer heads.

This deck is also one of the best users of Unfair Stamp in the current format. You primarily play with a single-Prize board in the early game, and the opponent KOing Budew often results in them getting Unfair Stamped. This deck combines multiple pieces of disruption together with Crushing Hammer, Unfair Stamp and Boss's Orders alongside Phantom Dive on something like a Fezandipiti or Latias ex without taking a KO, forcing the opponent to find multiple cards to KO the Dragapult without the assistance of Flip the Script. If your opponent just hits the Dragapult without taking the knockout, you often win the game immediately thanks to having so much damage to move over to their side with Munkidori. Judge also functions as another disruption card for this deck. While Judge is not as good as Special Red Card in the aggressive matchups, it's often for breaking stalemates where both players are building cards in hand and you want to initiate without fear of retaliation from a potential Unfair Stamp and Crushing Hammers. There are several lists of this deck that also have Special Red Card alongside Unfair Stamp and Judge, but I don't think that Special Red Card is currently necessary.

The only real card slot is flexible in this deck is the third copy of Darkness Energy. There are many options to play in this slot, including Dudunsparce ex to answer Big Basic decks, Special Red Card as extra disruption, Jamming Tower as an extra Stadium bump and Psychic Energy to use Mind Bend more often. However, I like Darkness Energy since it's slightly better in the Dragapult mirror match, which is very important in the current format. Having more Munkidori than your opponent in that matchup is very important to control the damage in play and you can often win from multiple Prize cards down by having more access to Adrena-Brain throughout the game.

Dragapult ex is very popular right now, which has resulted in many of the other decks warping their strategy around countering it. Even though its internal game plan is so flexible, many of the decks you play against will feel like difficult matchups but even the seemingly difficult matchups like Basic Box, Hide & Sneak and Crustle are all very doable with the right game plan. When playing this deck, it's very important to be open minded about your decisions. Just because you're able to use Phantom Dive doesn't mean that it's correct to do so, and just because you're able to play Unfair Stamp doesn't mean that it's the best turn for it. You ideally want to play Unfair Stamp on a turn where you force your opponent to draw multiple cards for their ideal turn. Playing Unfair Stamp in the early game just to use Itchy Pollen is usually very weak as your opponent has multiple turns to draw out of the two cards, and this often turns into five cards by the time they need to play any cards to KO a potential Dragapult ex.

Despite Dragapult's reputation as not being fun to play against, it has produced some of the most interesting and dynamic games I've played in the current format. Regardless of which side is using Phantom Dive, the game will usually be interesting and have a ton of decisions to it, and I'm excited to see where this deck goes for the rest of its longevity in the Standard format!

item.title: Everything You Missed from the Flesh and Blood World Championship
item.description:
Flesh and Blood|Classic Constructed|competitive|news

Everything You Missed from the Flesh and Blood World Championship

The largest Flesh and Blood events of all time with the most diverse metagame of the year so far!

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Nov 12, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

I've said it before, I'll say it again: World Championships are built different — and not just because they're the biggest event of the year.  

There's just something more tangible about a World Championship. I've tried to explain the pedigree required to conquer a Pro Tour to my extended family, and they just don't get it... but a World Championship? That has real life parallels. Everybody can understand that you are amongst the best on the planet at whichever craft you've dedicated yourself to and I think that's quite special.  

That's why I don't miss World Championships. In Flesh and Blood's case, I've played two and worked on three. 

The most recent of these was this past weekend in Paris, France. Perhaps more importantly, the event set a new expectation for the future of Flesh and Blood in more ways than one. Both the World Championship itself and the corresponding Calling featured the largest attendance numbers of all time, with the latter boasting over 1400 players in the event.  

That's to say nothing about the fistful of announcements. The World Championship Keynote added some clarity to the previous FaB 3.0 announcements, revealed additional cards from upcoming booster set Outbreak, announced the dates of every World Tour event in 2027 and confirmed both the names and aesthetics of almost every product releasing next year. It's a lot to take in. 

Throw in great players and better games, and we found ourselves with a weekend you couldn't afford to miss. I was honoured to be bringing you the action from the commentary booth all weekend, but I'm not offended if you weren't lucky enough to find yourself in Paris. Hop on over to the official FABTCG YouTube Channel to watch back the coverage of each event or check out the rest of this article to learn more about all the things you missed from the Flesh and Blood World Championship.

The Keynote

Shall we go chronologically? It seems only logical to me.  

Every Tier 4 event features a hotly anticipated keynote speech by either Legend Story Studios CEO James White or Head of Game Design and Development Bryan Gottlieb. These speeches are designed to give the community a small taste of what to expect in the future and reveal key information about upcoming releases.  

The texture of this looked a little different heading into the World Championship this year. FaB 3.0 and Outbreak had been revealed prior to this, so what on earth did the team have left in the chamber to reveal?! 

We kicked off the show with a closer look at every hero debuting in Outbreak. Whisper Shot, Kickback and Rocket-Powered Arrow stand out as SAGE legal signposts for the hybrid classes, while Eidetic Endpoint and Change of Mind strike me as backbreakingly powerful for Vyle, Catalyst of Collapse and Min, Genius // Min, Mad. These heroes are looking very well-round out of the gate and that's quite exciting.

But Outbreak was far from the only product getting reveals. Armory Deck: Min and the freshly announced Mastery Pack: Brute had some goodies to give. Zuul, Clubcaste and Babaza, Bloodbeat Heartfather are two new Brute heroes entering alongside the pack, dipping into design space that the class has been underserved in since they were introduced: club synergies and the Beat Chest keyword.

Beat of Savagery stands out as potentially being quite scary, but I've got my eyes on Tenderized. Not only is the name kind of gnarly, but I do not want to be dealing with a six-power attack that'll have four or more additional damage stapled onto it sometimes. Messy stuff.  

Next, we saw the full list of World Tour dates for 2026. As alluded to in FaB 3.0, there would be less events this year in exchange for a hearty bump in prize money across the board.  That means fifteen events instead of thirty-six: a significant drop.  

Truthfully, I think this is a good thing. Events were arguably too frequently this year to the point of being missable. This should allow every event to feel more prestigious and offer more bang for your buck if you're playing for prizes. It sucks for exactly me given I'll be hired to be in the booth less, but beyond that I'm a big fan.  

The full schedule is now available on the FABTCG events page, so go check it out! 

Amongst a selection of other promo cards, we also found ourselves with the full product roadmap for 2027. One Lotus and Ancients Awaken were plenty suggestive of their themes in logos alone, but the team at Legend Story Studios didn't want to leave it at that.  

No. We got confirmation that Dromai and Iyslander will be returning within these sets. 

Let me tell you. I cried.  

Iyslander was the hero I piloted in both of my World Championship appearances. I am absolutely buzzing to defrost my career and take on the best alongside my original ride-or-die. Based on the eruption in the room, I feel many people felt the same! James even politely suggested that more heroes would be returning in these sets — you'll just have to stay tuned to find out who.  

It's a good year to be a Flesh and Blood player if you ask me. Get me to Philadelphia already.  

The Metagame

As previously mentioned, both the Calling and World Championship in Paris were the largest ever versions of their respective tournament type. Almost 600 players rocked the show in the main event, while just under 1500 took to the arena over in the Calling.  

The metagames were almost mirrored when the events began. Fang, Dracai of Blades and Levia, Shadowborn Abomination wrestled for the most represented deck, with the draconic warrior coming out on top by just a handful of copies in both cases. Jarl Vetreidi, Ser Boltyn, Breaker of Dawn and Aurora, Legacy of Tempest fleshed out the remaining spots in our weird five-sided triangle.

It was an entirely different tale by the time the smoke cleared, though. In the World Championship, the Warrior class dominated affairs. Fang, Dracai of Blades continued to burn bright as one of the more resilient, powerful decks in the format, but Ser Boltyn, Olympia, Prized Fighter and a heavily anti-Warrior teched variant of Dorinthea Ironsong would also manage to make the top cut alongside a pair of Gravy Bones, Shipwrecked Looter.

In the Calling? Zero Warriors. Not even any copies of Levia. Instead, we found ourselves staring at some well-rounded aggressive decks and the most defensive stonewalls you've ever seen. Nine copies of Staunch Response in each of these Jarl Vetreidi decks, would you believe? 

I think people are underselling the return of Gravy Bones, Shipwrecked Looter considering these results. It's easy to get distracted by the wall of warrior or unbreakable defenses of Jarl and Teklo, but it was the only hero to appear in the top cut of both events despite being the sixth most played deck on both occasions. One to watch as far as I'm concerned.  

Either way, it's clear that the metagame remains largely unsolved in the wake of these two events. Even better, we've got Mastery Pack: Assassin and Outbreak on the horizon. Who knows what things will look like in the near future?  

If you'd like to see any of the top decklists from across the weekend, you can find them all below: 

The Winners

When the smoke cleared, Canada's Nicolas Jamoulle stood tall as the 2026 Flesh and Blood World Champion, achieving an incredible record of 16-3 between draft and Classic Constructed. He even had to conquer one of those losses when he met Jin Han Toh for the second time in the final for the Fang, Dracai of Blades mirror match.

Fang is a reasonably solved commodity at this point, but Jamoulle had some interesting inclusions. It's typically quite difficult to make space for everything once you decide you're interested in the slightly more explosive turns offered by Perforate — but those extra dagger swings made all the difference in Jamoulle's semi-final match. What do you trim instead? 

All the tech cards, it seems. No Balance of Justice. No Warmonger's Diplomacy. Heck, no Tooth of the Dragon even. Jamoulle came to the party convinced that the core pieces of Fang were all the power he needed. He just had to make sure it happened consistently.  

In the Calling, Matt Muus would take down a second Calling title on Teklovossen, Esteemed Magnate. Nobody else can seem to find the same level of success on this deck as Muus, but he looked untouchable in his finals clash against Cody Gebert. Three copies of Jarl Vetreidi standing between you and glory? Elementary, my dear Watson. 

A couple of cool spots here that I'd really like to call out. First of all, bringing the full suite of Proto Base equipment ended up paying off in spades when Gebert attempted to shatter Muus's arm slot with Frozen to Death. Fabricate kept the possibility of Singularity on the table despite it not being required.  

But I'm most enamored by Exorcism. The card is primarily here to line up with one of your overpower attacks against Levia, Shadowborn Abomination and get that robust banish zone turned faced down, but it has some incidental splash damage against Jarl players that are still relying on Felling of the Crown or other decompose effects. It's a heads-up choice from Muus that you should be aware of going forward if you're staring down Teklovossen.

Closing Thoughts

It was an honor and a pleasure to be so deeply involved in the 2026 Flesh and Blood World Championship. It was a wonderful event with some emotional storylines. Where else can you find an up-and-coming newer player staring down a FaB Dad for six figures of prize money?  

I can only hope to see you at the next one. Until then, feel free to hit me up at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky! Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game.

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing!

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!   

Written By

Scott Mines

Scott "HowlingMines" Mines is a seventeen year veteran of the TCG industry, having done everything from serving coffee at LGSs to battling the best on the World Championship stage. Now ... View Full Bio

item.title: The Most Valuable One Piece Cards You Can Open in Packs Right Now
item.description:
One Piece|collecting|finance

The Most Valuable One Piece Cards You Can Open in Packs Right Now

Treasures ahoy!

By Ken Nishi

|

Published Nov 12, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

One of the biggest appeals of the One Piece Card Game is the sheer number of valuable cards waiting to be pulled from booster packs. From beautiful alternate-art versions of fan-favorite characters to some of the rarest collectibles in the game, there's always something exciting to chase after. Even though you could simply purchase the singles individually, it's a different feeling entirely to pull the card from a pack that you opened yourself.

While some of the biggest and most recognizable hits come from older releases, newer sets continue to introduce cards that quickly find their way onto collectors' wishlists. Today's newest releases might only be a few months old, but before long, they'll be several years old themselves, and players will be looking to track down the cards they missed.

With EB-05 now added to the mix, it's a good time to revisit the biggest pulls available across the One Piece Card Game. Let's take a look at the most sought-after One Piece cards you can find when opening packs today!

Heroines Edition Vol.2 (EB-05)

Extra Booster: One Piece Heroines Edition Vol. 2 (EB-05) is the latest release for the One Piece Card Game, and it's yet another set packed with cards celebrating some of the franchise's most popular female characters. The set features a wide variety of characters, including Nami, Nico Robin, Boa Hancock, Yamato, and Perona, alongside several other fan favorites. With new alternate arts, special SP printings, and some especially rare cards, there's plenty for players and collectors to get excited about.

The most desirable cards in the set are undoubtedly those with new special treatments. One of the most expensive is the gold-stamped Nami, illustrated by Kentaro Yabuki, which has quickly become one of the most sought-after cards in the game. There's also a Super Leader Alternate Art Nico Robin, featuring a Manga Rare-style treatment of the set's new Leader, as well as Manga Rare Shirahoshi. All three are incredibly difficult pulls, but they're exactly the kind of cards that make opening Heroines Edition Vol. 2 so exciting.

Beyond those massive hits, EB-05 has a ton of different SP cards featuring characters from across the One Piece series. These include new versions of new and existing cards like Nami, Boa Hancock, and Vinsmoke Reiju.

The World's Strongest Warriors (OP-17)

The World's Strongest Warriors celebrates the fourth anniversary of the One Piece Card Game by featuring the original Four Emperors alongside characters from the Elbaph arc.

The ultimate chases in the set are the Pirate Crew Rares! Taking inspiration from the Red Manga Rare cards introduced in OP-13, OP-17 features two incredibly rare Pirate Crew Rares, showcasing either Luffy or Rocks alongside their respective crews. These are undoubtedly some of the most difficult cards to find in the entire game, and pulling either one would be an incredible hit.

Of course, the Pirate Crew Rares aren't the only major attractions in OP-17. The set also introduces four Manga Rares featuring the original Four Emperors: Whitebeard, Big Mom, Kaido, and Shanks. There's even a special alternate-art version of Monkey.D.Luffy designed in the Manga Rare style!

Beyond that, there are a variety of SP cards, as well as alternate-art versions of popular characters and event cards, giving players great collectible cards to pull, despite not reaching the astronomical prices of the set's main chases. With such a diverse array of cards you can pull, The World's Strongest Warriors is certainly worth checking out.

The Time of Battle (OP-16)

The Time of Battle draws heavily from the Marineford and Impel Down story arcs. Between its three Manga Rares, a collection of SP cards, and an assortment of desirable alternate arts, there are plenty of cards worth chasing in OP-16.

The biggest hits are undoubtedly the three Manga Rares featuring Borsalino, Sakazuki, and Kuzan. Each card showcases one of the three Admirals who played a major role during the Paramount War, with the iconic manga panels in their respective backgrounds. Since all three cards share a matching artistic theme, they're particularly appealing to anyone looking to complete the entire collection.

OP-16 also features several SP cards with a distinctive portrait-style design, placing each character front and center against a relatively simple background. Ms. All Sunday is easily the standout of the group, commanding a considerably higher price than the other SP cards. However, Portgas.D.Ace, Charlotte Katakuri, and Tashigi are also solid pulls, giving the set several additional collectibles for players and fans to chase.

Adventure on Kami's Island (OP15-EB04)

Adventure on Kami's Island (OP-15) brings together characters from the Sky Island and Dressrosa story arcs alongside several cards originally introduced in the Japanese-only set Egghead Crisis (EB-04). The set has a nice mix of desirable rarities and popular characters, with its Manga Rares and SP cards still being exciting pulls.

The two biggest chase cards are the Manga Rares featuring and Koby](product-hover id="" noConvert="true"). Enel is the more expensive of the two, largely thanks to its history as a competitive staple and continued demand from players. Koby may not reach quite the same heights, but it's still a valuable collectible and another difficult Manga Rare to pull.

Beyond those two cards, OP-15 also features two different SP cycles, with Monkey.D.Luffy](product-hover id="685194" noConvert="true") and Boa Hancock standing out as the most valuable options. Zeus is another notable hit, maintaining strong demand thanks to its usefulness in competitive decks.

One Piece Heroines Edition (EB-03)

One Piece Heroines Edition is the predecessor to Heroines Edition Vol. 2, and likewise puts the spotlight on some of the franchise's most popular female characters. With a lineup featuring fan favorites like Nami, Nico Robin, Boa Hancock, and Uta, the set has continued to be extremely popular with collectors. It has an unusually strong selection of expensive cards, making it an especially attractive product to crack open for anyone hoping to pull something valuable.

One interesting thing about EB-03 is that its most expensive cards aren't actually its Manga Rare. Instead, several of the SP cards have become the biggest prizes in the set, with Nami, Boa Hancock, and Nico Robin all reaching prices above $1,000. The popularity of these characters has helped push their SP versions to remarkable prices, while Nami and Nico Robin also benefit from their playability. Other SP cards featuring Nefeltari Vivi, Perona, and Uta are still worth a pretty penny, as well!

That doesn't mean the set's Manga Rare should be overlooked, though. Uta remains a highly desirable card, combining one of the game's most recognizable rarities with a particularly popular character. Although it currently falls short of the three biggest SP cards in terms of market value, it's still an impressive pull and an important part of the set's appeal.

Overall, Heroines Edition stands out for having valuable cards spread across several different rarities, making it one of the more rewarding One Piece products to open.

The Azure Sea's Seven (OP14-EB03)

The Azure Sea's Seven (OP-14) kicked off the One Piece Card Game's 2026 booster lineup, offering a diverse selection of collectible cards, ranging from special anniversary-style treatments to Manga Rares, SPs, and Alternate Arts.

The biggest prizes in OP-14 are its special Gold and Silver versions of OP09-051 Buggy. These cards finish a collection that started with the game's third anniversary, which introduced Gold and Silver versions of Monkey.D.Luffy in A Fist of Divine Speed (OP-11), Marshall.D.Teach in Legacy of the Master (OP-12), and Shanks in Carrying On His Will (OP-13). With Buggy now joining the lineup, collectors can finally complete the Gold and Silver collection featuring all of the new Four Emperors. Neither version is easy to pull, but that makes them that much more desirable!

There are several other impressive pulls to look out for, too. OP-14 features a Manga Rare Dracule Mihawk, a particularly desirable collectible given his former importance as a boss monster in Mihawk strategies. The set also has some valuable SP cards, with Roronoa Zoro and Boa Hancock leading the way.

The 10 Most Expensive Pokémon Chase Cards in Delta Reign

Everybody loves Rayquaza.

By Peter Day

|

Published Nov 10, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

With Delta Reign, the Pokémon Company International is closing out 2026 by continuing the trends we saw throughout the year.

Like Perfect Order, Chaos Rising, and Pitch Black before it, Delta Reign is a relatively small English Pokémon set based on a single Japanese expansion, with one massive headliner as the set's singular focus. This time, that headliner is Rayquaza, a fan-favorite Pokémon on a level beyond that of Zygarde, Greninja, and Darkrai.

As expected, the Special Illustration Rare (SIR) and Mega Hyper Rare (MHR) versions of the Sky-High Pokémon have soared far above everything else in Delta Reign. That doesn't mean you can write off the rest of the set, however. While the other SIRs don't have anything close to Rayquaza's name recognition, more than a few of the Illustration Rares (IRs) in Delta Reign have ascended to chase status—either because the Pokémon they feature are so iconic, or for Tomokazu Komiya reasons.

Let's take a look at some of the Illustration Rares and Special Illustration Rares that are vying to be Rayquaza's opening act. These are the most valuable Pokémon cards in Delta Reign.

#10 Mega Golisopod ex 135/103 (Special Illustration Rare)

Debuting in cardboard for the first time in Delta Reign, Mega Golisopod ex has a swanky Special Illustration Rare version by prolific Pokémon artist nagimiso, and an attack that's just as appealing. With Finishing Blow, Mega Golisopod ex can deal 220 damage for a single Energy as long as its victim has any damage counters on it already.

Is that strong enough to see play? We'll have to wait until after Dragapult retires from ruling the format to find out. In the meantime, this card's harsh purple, orange, and green color scheme ensures that it stands out.

#9 Groudon 111/103 (Illustration Rare)

Rayquaza may be the star of Delta Reign, but the other two members of the weather trio haven't been left out. The Continent Pokémon Groudon appears as an Illustration Rare in the set, and the Sea Basin Pokémon Kyogre cameos as the promo card that comes with Delta Reign Elite Trainer Boxes.

Ryota Murayama's blazing-hot illustration adds a third contender for the title of the best-looking full-art Groudon card ever printed, alongside Nurikabe's IR Groudon from Paradox Rift and nagimiso's Team Magma's Groudon-EX. Both of those cards have topped their respective sets' price guides in the past, so it's not surprising that this Groudon has become one of the big chase cards in Delta Reign.

#8 Aarune 139/103 (Special Illustration Rare)

With his ability to grab multiple Stadium cards, Aarune works great in decks that want to assemble both halves of a Legendary Stadium like Legendary Pyroduct.

That's nifty, but it's not enough to make every Aarune card valuable, as evidenced by his Ultra Rare and Uncommon versions. I also wouldn't attribute the price difference solely to this card's (admittedly adorable) artwork by Shimaris Yukichi.

As far as this card's price goes, its most significant trait is just its Special Illustration Rare (SIR) rarity, typically the most-sought after rarity in modern Pokémon sets. Pokémon fans love high rarities, and art with actual backgrounds, and SIRs check both of those boxes.

#7 Mega Golurk ex 137/103 (Special Illustration Rare)

Mega Golurk is another Mega-Evolved Pokémon that's getting its TCG debut in Delta Reign after appearing in Pokémon Legends: Z-A.

Goliath's Punch comes with too many restrictions and drawbacks to make it appealing to players. Thankfully, the art is attractive enough on its own. Takeshi Nakamura chose the perfect blend of sunset colors to make Mega Golurk's high-contrast yellow-and-purple color scheme look natural, even dignified.

Golurk might not be the highest-profile Pokémon in the franchise, but everyone knows a gorgeous card when they see one.

#6 Zinnia's Trust 140/103 (Special Illustration Rare)

Zinnia earned the respect of Pokémon fans with her determined pursuit of Rayquaza in order to save the planet in Delta Episode.

As a mysterious woman connected to a fan-favorite Pokémon, Zinnia has been an immensely popular character in the franchise, and many of the cards featuring her have been as valuable as that fact implies. Now Zinnia fans have another card to chase like the fate of the world is at stake.

#5 Eevee 114/103 (Illustration Rare)

From Growlithe to Azurill to Sprigatito, Delta Reign has an impressive lineup of Illustration Rares featuring beloved Pokémon. But none of them compare to Eevee, the pre-evolution to everyone's favorite Pokémon. (All eight of them).

Eevee has appeared on countless valuable Pokémon cards over the years, and this Illustration Rare continues the trend. Hideki Ishikawa didn't stray too far from the standard Pokémon style guide with this card, but they showed impressive attention to detail with the dappled sunlight and the stitching on the bag.

Most importantly though, this card shows Eevee in the kind of pose that would earn any pet a devoted social media following. Cute things are cute.

#4 Kecleon 117/103 (Illustration Rare)

Who would even think to draw a Kecleon pole-dancing in a kaleidoscopic rain forest? Only Tomokazu Komiya.

Komiya uses colors, poses, and backgrounds that wouldn't even occur to a less creative artist. His idiosyncratic style has earned his work a lot of well-deserved attention over the years, and that attention has translated into hype for cards with his name on them—especially the most outlandish ones. No surprise that his latest Crayola fever dream has found an audience.

#3 Raikou ex 136/103 (Mega Hyper Rare)

Rayquaza's not the only Legendary Pokémon with a Special Illustration Rare card in Delta Reign. The Thunder Pokémon Raikou also has an SIR, with a stunning illustration by Oku where Raikou appears to be riding lightning down from the mountains.

For a Legendary Gen II Pokémon, Raikou hasn't appeared in many full-art cards over the years, and arguably none of them look as dynamic as this one. Raikou deserved a glow-up like this.

#2 Mega Rayquaza ex 141/103 (Mega Hyper Rare)

Since the start of the Mega Evolution Series in late 2025, every Pokémon set has had one or two gold-colored Mega Hyper Rare cards as their capstones. These are the rarest cards in their respective sets, and while they're not usually the most valuable (fans don't love the monochromatic artwork), their scarcity alone makes them incredibly valuable.

In Delta Reign, the Pokémon that got the Mega Hyper Rare treatment was none other than Mega Rayquaza ex, the set's mascot and strongest new attacker. Obviously, the gold-tinted version of the Pokémon on all the box art was always going to be one of the biggest chase cards in the set.

Just, not the biggest.

#1 Mega Rayquaza ex 138/103 (Special Illustration Rare)

By far, the most expensive Pokémon card in Delta Reign is Special Illustration Rare Mega Rayquaza ex.

Delta Reign is Rayquaza's set, and no version of Mega Rayquaza ex has collectors more excited than the SIR. That largely comes down to the art. While the Mega Hyper Rare version feels opulent, modern Pokémon collectors tend to prefer cards with actual backgrounds that show characters as living parts of the Pokémon world, not as static mascots. And Kazuki Minami's take on Mega Rayquaza is about as far from static as you can get (though it's plenty electric, har har), showing the Sky-High Pokémon in a moment of dynamic exuberance that jolts the viewer awake.
